extracted.intended_audience: journalists, media critics and informed readers interested in BBC reporting and the Hutton Inquiry
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and reporting on the accuracy, sourcing and phrasing of high‑profile broadcast journalism (using the BBC/Hutton/David Kelly episode as the case study). Focuses on source verification, attribution, headline proportionality and editorial process understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise attribution of claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Attribute claims to the correct actors and levels of certainty rather than using vague labels like 'the government'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author gives an explicit example of a better attribution: ‘The 45 minute claim was included in the dossier against the wishes of some experts from defence intelligence, who thought Downing St was responsible for doing so’. This contrasts with looser phrasing that implies ministerial responsibility when the disagreement was within the civil service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify whether source was in a position to know
rubrics_metrics.description: Check whether a named source actually had the role, access or standing to know the fact they are alleged to know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece criticises Gilligan for not checking that David Kelly was 'in a position to know' (Kelly fed into the JIC process and was not a JIC member). Guidance/anti-pattern: do not accept a source's speculation about others' actions without confirming their proximity to the facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient sourcing for broadcast
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure claims meet producer guidelines on sourcing before broadcasting; insufficiently sourced material should not be aired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The comment notes that 'under BBC producer guidelines the whole story was insufficiently sourced to be broadcast.' Use multiple corroborating sources and meet institutional sourcing thresholds for broadcast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sensational or disproportionate headlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Headlines should reflect the strength of the evidence and not be crafted primarily for shock value or political convenience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author contrasts the dossier's careful (but weak) evidence with tabloid headlines like 'BRITS 45mins FROM DOOM', warning against inflating limited or ambiguous material to generate headlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be specific about institutional actors (civil service vs ministers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between disagreements within the civil service and actions by ministers or political advisers; don't conflate 'the government' with ministers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: David Boothroyd's comment highlights how the word 'government' would be commonly understood to mean ministers, whereas in the Hutton case the concerns remained within the civil service; clarity here materially changes the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not present speculation or naming as fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat a source's speculative identification of individuals as speculation unless independently verified; avoid presenting it as established fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Gilligan accepted Kelly's naming of Alastair Campbell as personally responsible; the author notes Kelly had no direct knowledge and this should have been handled as speculation, not evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify ambiguous phrases rather than assuming a single meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: When using or reporting ambiguous terms (e.g., 'sexed up'), explain or paraphrase the intended meaning instead of assuming a single legalistic interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author criticises Hutton for adopting a narrow meaning of 'sexed up' (as 'embellished with false or unreliable items') and argues the phrase can validly cover weaker assertions; journalists should avoid leaving such phrases ambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent statement of evidence strength
rubrics_metrics.description: Convey clearly the limits, quality and provenance of the evidence (e.g., 'limited, patchy, superficial and poorly sourced' rather than 'extensive, detailed and authoritative').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author contrasts political statements that presented intelligence as 'extensive, detailed and authoritative' with the reality; reporters should make the true strength and limits of intelligence clear to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check consistency and phrasing of claims across documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Note when a claim appears in multiple inconsistent formulations (the dossier phrased the 45‑minute claim in four different ways) and assess whether that inconsistency weakens the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inconsistent wording can be a clue to a weak or poorly founded claim; reporters and editors should flag inconsistent formulations rather than amplify them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroborate major allegations with process-level investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate the process by which a document was compiled (who fed in what, who overruled whom) rather than relying solely on individual anecdotes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author says a stronger story would have examined the compilation process of the dossier and who had responsibility; this requires checking committee membership, document trails and official roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish personal opinion from organizational position
rubrics_metrics.description: Make clear when commentary is an individual's personal view and not a position adopted by the organization publishing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author explicitly notes 'This is my personal opinion... It was not a position adopted by the BBC.' Journalists and bloggers should similarly label personal analysis versus institutional statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand editorial structures before judging them
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure critics and inquiries understand newsroom/editorial processes and responsibilities before making definitive criticisms of editorial structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues Hutton made ill‑founded criticisms of BBC editorial structures because he 'didn't understand' them; evaluators should seek to learn internal processes (and call witnesses if needed) before concluding structural fault.
